name: Gareth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Gareth. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead lineman out of the Brookfield depot, inland, farm country. Mostly it's rural lines, long single runs out to farms, so a lot of driving on gravel roads, climbing wooden poles, changing crossarms and fuses, and clearing branches off the wires. When there's a storm, you go until it's fixed. That's the job.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside and I like that people are glad to see you. An old farmer once gave me a whole lamb after we got his milking shed back on in a blizzard. What wears me out is the pay, which isn't great for what we do, and the paperwork they keep piling on. I'm not a screens person.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you handle the paperwork, then?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write it out by hand and my second, Stan, puts it in the system. I've got a basic phone, calls and texts. Kezia, my girlfriend, says I'm the last man alive without apps, and she's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much. Probably something like, well, the world's still turning. I don't post online, so it'd just be a shrug at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is, I'd be happy. I don't use any of it and I don't want to. If it all comes to nothing, I keep climbing poles and nobody makes me learn a new app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Turn up, do the job, keep paying off what's left of the loan for my dad's funeral, which should be done by next autumn. Maybe then start putting a bit away for a place of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as any other week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where are you and Kezia living right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the annex behind her parents' house. It's one room and a little kitchen, but the rent's cheap, and her dad lets me use his shed for fixing my truck. It's fine for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a place of your own look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing fancy. A small house on the edge of town with a yard for a dog and space to park the truck. Kezia wants a vegetable garden, I want a workbench. That's about it.

S0.say: I'd say not much, probably just that the world's still turning. I don't post online, so it'd be a shrug at the depot.
S0.think: I'd be happy, because I don't use any of it and I don't want to. If it comes to nothing, I keep climbing poles and nobody makes me learn a new app.
S0.do: Keeps working as usual and finishes paying off the loan for his father's funeral by next autumn. Then starts saving a little towards a place of his own with his girlfriend.
S0.quote: If it all comes to nothing, I keep climbing poles and nobody makes me learn a new app.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is a man of few words who avoids technology entirely and is proud of it. Money is tight because of a loan for his father's funeral, and he and his girlfriend live cheaply in her parents' annex. His goals are simple and concrete: a small house, a dog and a workbench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business. If a drone can check a line cheaper than a man in a truck, they'll use the drone. I wouldn't moan about it in public, no point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it bothers me more than I'd say. If the job turns into flying drones and tapping screens, I'm not the guy for that. I'm the guy you want on a pole at midnight in the rain, but I don't know how long they'll pay for that if everything else goes digital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep doing good work, because being the best on the crew is the only card I've got. I'd wait and see what they bring in before I panic. If they made a course compulsory, I'd do it, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the truck engine you're hoping goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said being the best is your only card. What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't have savings, I don't have a degree, and there's no other depot near Brookfield. So the only reason they'd keep me over someone else is that I'm good. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at work help you with the screen side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stan would, he already does. But I'd feel like a passenger, and I don't like that. I'd rather be the one carrying people.

S1.say: I'd say it's business, and if a drone can check a line cheaper than a man in a truck, they'll use the drone. I wouldn't moan about it in public.
S1.think: It bothers me more than I'd say, because if the job turns into drones and screens, I'm not the guy for that. I don't know how long they'll pay for a man on a pole at midnight.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and keeps doing excellent work as his main protection. Waits to see what the company brings in and would only take a course if it were made compulsory.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a noise in the truck engine he hopes will go away.
S1.quote: I'm the guy you want on a pole at midnight in the rain, but I don't know how long they'll pay for that if everything else goes digital.
S1.fieldNote: His public line is a shrug about business, but privately he is worried about being left behind by screens. He sees his skill as his only card, with no savings, degree or nearby alternatives. Relying on Stan for the digital side clearly hurts his pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing in public. At the depot I'd say we're all in the same boat, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be done. Two years, no savings, no other depot, no screen skills, and every other job round here would be getting hit too, the feed store, the farms, the lot. I'd have nothing to fall back on, and I mean nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up until they tell me not to, because what else would I do. I'd stop all spending except food and petrol and finish the funeral loan as fast as I could. I'd ask Kezia's parents if we could stay in the annex rent-free for a while, which would be hard to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. I can feel my stomach going just talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kezia that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't have a plan, and that's the first time I've ever said that to her. She'd probably say we'll sort it out. She's better at that than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at all two years would let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Two years isn't enough to save, and it's not enough for me to turn into a computer guy, even if I wanted to. It's just enough time to watch it come.

S2.say: I'd probably say nothing in public. At the depot I'd just say we're all in the same boat.
S2.think: I'd be done, with two years, no savings, no other depot and no screen skills. Every other job round here would be getting hit too, so I'd have nothing to fall back on.
S2.do: Keeps turning up for work until told otherwise and cuts all spending except food and petrol. Rushes to pay off the funeral loan and asks his girlfriend's parents if they can stay in the annex rent-free.
S2.feel: Panicked, with his stomach turning just talking about it.
S2.quote: I'd say I don't have a plan, and that's the first time I've ever said that to her.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario leaves him with no options he can see, and he admits it plainly. He would keep working out of habit and lean on his girlfriend's family. The line about having no plan was clearly hard for him to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, I wouldn't say much. Maybe I'd say we've got a few years, let's see what the company does. I'm not one for speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years doesn't fix much for me. I'd still have no savings to speak of and I'd still hate screens. It just gives me five years of worrying instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to save, properly this time, even a hundred a month. I'd cut out the fishing trips and the pub on Fridays. And I'd probably still wait to see what the company offers before learning anything new, because I've seen them change their minds a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Not as bad as the fast one, but it's still there every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the company. What if they never offer anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have wasted the time, I know. Kezia would be on at me to do something. I'd probably end up asking Stan what courses he's doing and tagging along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years change anything about your plans with Kezia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house would wait. No point signing a mortgage if the job's going. We'd stay in the annex and keep saving, and I'd feel bad about it every time she looks at house listings.

S3.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe just that we've got a few years so let's see what the company does. I'm not one for speeches.
S3.think: Five years doesn't fix much for me, because I'd still have no savings to speak of and still hate screens. It just gives me five years of worrying instead of two.
S3.do: Tries to save at least a hundred a month by cutting fishing trips and Friday pub nights. Waits to see what the company offers before learning anything new, and puts off buying a house.
S3.feel: Alarmed, less sharply than the fast version but there every night.
S3.quote: It just gives me five years of worrying instead of two.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't feel useful to him because he doesn't plan to change much with it. He admits his wait-and-see habit could waste the years. The house plan is the real casualty, and he feels guilty about his girlfriend's hopes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, plenty can happen. People round here would say the same. Most of us would probably just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the one I could live with. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd have ten good years on the poles, which is more than some guys get anyway because of their backs. And by then maybe I'd have something saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save steadily. I'd finish the loan, then put money into a savings account Kezia would make me open. If the company made a robot supervision course compulsory in a few years, I'd do it then, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It feels far enough away to sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd only learn new things if forced. Why is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time I've tried a new system, it's made me look stupid in front of the crew. I'm good at what I do, and I'd rather not be bad at something in public. I know that's not a great reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with the other two AGI pictures for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm finished. Five, I'm worried every day. Ten, I can just about see myself at the end of it, still in a hi-vis vest, maybe telling the robot where to go.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can happen. Most of us round here would just get on with it.
S4.think: It's the one I could live with, because I'd have ten good years on the poles and maybe something saved. That's more than some guys get anyway because of their backs.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves steadily once the funeral loan is paid. Plans to take a robot supervision course only if the company makes it compulsory in a few years.
S4.feel: Anxious, but able to breathe because it feels far enough away to sleep.
S4.quote: I'm good at what I do, and I'd rather not be bad at something in public.
S4.fieldNote: His resistance to new tools turns out to be about pride and fear of looking foolish, which he admitted openly. Ten years gives him room to picture himself still working. He still wouldn't act unless pushed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. That one, I've got no answer for. What would help is someone, the company or whoever, telling us straight what the plan is for the crews, and giving people like me time and pay to learn the new stuff without feeling like idiots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the small towns. Brookfield is the depot, the feed store and the school. If the depot goes, I don't know what's left to keep people here.

headlineQuote: If the depot goes, I don't know what's left to keep people here.
portrait: Gareth Mensah is a 27-year-old lead lineman at a rural inland depot, a quiet, skilled man who climbs wooden poles on long farm runs and has never used an app. He's paying off a loan for his father's funeral and lives cheaply in the annex behind his girlfriend Kezia's parents' house. He shrugs off the slow scenarios in public but privately fears being left behind by screens, and the two-year AGI picture leaves him panicked with no plan at all. More warning time mostly means more worry for him, because he'd wait for the company to act, though ten years lets him picture getting through.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, which he says he has no answer for.
whatWouldHelp: A straight plan for the crews from the company or whoever is in charge, plus time and pay to learn new skills without feeling foolish.
